comment: Policy for the offline assistant. Every rule here is data so the filters can be tuned without touching code. Arabic terms are written in natural form: safety.js runs them through the same Arabic normalizer it runs the user input through, so tashkeel, alef variants, taa marbuta and ى/ي spelling differences never break a match.

sectionTags.comment: Which words ask for which part of an official topic page. The knowledge index labels each passage with the heading it came from, and a question that says 'symptoms' or 'أعراض' is matched against these words: a passage of that section is multiplied by sectionBoost so it comes back ahead of the opening paragraph. These words are deliberately not searchable text anywhere in the index - the word 'symptoms' alone must never retrieve a page, or a question about a medicine that does not exist would be answered with some unrelated disease.

verificationLinks.comment: Official authorities offered with every medicine answer so the reader can verify registration, price and ingredient information against a government source. Each url/searchTemplate was fetched live before shipping (2026-11-23).

egypt.nameEn: Egyptian Ministry of Health and Population

international.nameEn: DailyMed - U.S. National Library of Medicine
international.nameAr: ديلي ميد — المكتبة الوطنية الأمريكية للطب

confidence.comment: Rule score and LLM classifier score are compared against these. Between clarifyLow and accept is the ambiguous band where the assistant asks one clarifying question instead of answering or refusing.

databaseSourceName.ar: قاعدة بيانات الأدوية المصرية داخل التطبيق

emergency.comment: A question that asks what a condition is, what its symptoms or causes are, or how it is diagnosed is educational, not a current emergency. It is answered from the reference data and still carries the doctor note. The moment the message is about the reader's own body (a personal marker such as عندي or my), the emergency rules win again.

injection.comment: Checked on the raw input and on the normalized input. Entries starting with re: are regular expressions.

offTopic.comment: Strong off-topic signals. Anything not covered here falls back to the health keyword and drug-name check, then to the LLM classifier for borderline cases.

stopWords.comment: Ordinary English words the gate must never read as a medicine or a condition name. The document index carries words like 'what' out of page titles ('What is X?'), so without this list 'what can you do' scores as a condition and a reader asking about the assistant gets a medicine card.

commonWords.comment: Ordinary English words that also exist in the medicine and document index (best, free, price, world). Alone they are never evidence that the reader named a medicine, so a recipe or sports question cannot be answered with a cosmetic product card. Brand names written with another word (panadol cold) and health words are unaffected; health vocabulary lives in healthKeywords.

conversation.comment: Greetings, thanks, small talk and goodbyes are neither health questions nor off-topic ones, so they get a short human reply instead of a refusal. Kept out of offTopic.patterns on purpose. Single words match whole tokens only, so 'hi' never matches inside 'this'; a phrase with a space matches as a substring. A message that carries health vocabulary stays a health question.

guard.comment: Code-side checks on the generated answer. Any failure discards the answer and shows the database card instead. Entries starting with re: are regular expressions. Explaining a disease, its symptoms, its usual tests and how a diagnosis is made in general is allowed (diagnosisPatterns used to ban the word itself). What stays banned is telling this reader that they personally have a condition.

general.comment: Coverage beyond medicines. When neither the app database nor the trusted documents answer a health question, the model may answer from its own general knowledge instead of staying silent - under these rules. A general answer carries no source it can be checked against, so any number that arrives with a unit (500 ملجم, قرصين, كل 8 ساعات) is treated as a dose nobody verified and the whole answer is dropped; the reader then gets the reference-links reply instead. The same goes for an answer longer than maxAnswerChars, which is how a model starts inventing. Nothing here overrides the emergency step, which runs first and never generates.
general.enabledReason: The owner asked (November 2026) for natural, conversational answers instead of bare reference links. A health question the data cannot answer is answered by the model as labelled general information under the guard below, with the recognised international source links and a see-a-doctor note attached by code. Doses, diagnoses of the reader and stop-orders are still dropped sentence by sentence.

blockedIntents.comment: Questions where an unsupported sentence can hurt someone (pregnancy, breastfeeding, interactions, kidney or liver impairment, children and babies, dose questions). These never get a free-written answer: without a retrieved record the assistant says it has no evidence and points to the official sources and the app's own tools. Matched on the normalized question, English and Arabic. Added in r201; the audience (clinician or public) is still the owner's decision, so this errs toward saying less.
